title: Yellow halos at the med pass
objective: Monitor digoxin for toxicity -- anorexia, nausea, vomiting, visual changes and dysrhythmias -- and remember low potassium and magnesium increase the risk

brief.situation: 08:00 on a medical unit. You are Mrs. Albright's nurse. She is 84, with heart failure and atrial fibrillation, admitted two days ago with pneumonia. Her morning medications are due, including the ordered digoxin and furosemide.
handover: She ate nothing at breakfast: 'I feel sick to my stomach, and the lights have yellow rings around them.'
This morning's labs posted at 07:30: you have not opened them yet. She weighs 48 kg.
Unit policy: an apical pulse for a full minute before digoxin; hold it and call the provider for a pulse under 60 or suspected toxicity; any RN may place a patient on telemetry while calling.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What explains her pulse and symptoms, why now, and what do you do with the morning digoxin?

parts.label: What and why now
parts.criteria: Digoxin toxicity: anorexia, nausea, vomiting, visual changes (yellow halos) and a slow, irregular pulse; risk raised by low potassium (on furosemide), worsening kidney function, age and low weight.
parts.modelAnswer: This looks like digoxin toxicity: no appetite, nausea, vomiting, yellow halos and a slow irregular pulse. Her potassium is low from the furosemide, her kidneys are worse, and she's 84 and 48 kg, which all raise the risk.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Holds the digoxin; places her on telemetry; calls the provider now for a level, magnesium and potassium replacement; does not give the dose with an antiemetic to cover the nausea.
parts.modelAnswer: Hold the digoxin, put her on telemetry and call the provider now for a level, magnesium and potassium. I don't give it with an antiemetic: the nausea is the warning.

block.headline: Heart block
block.body: Anorexia, nausea, visual changes and a slow irregular pulse on digoxin are toxicity until proved otherwise, especially with low potassium. Hold it, monitor, call.

caught.headline: Toxicity caught
caught.body: You took the apical pulse, connected her symptoms and potassium, held the digoxin, put her on telemetry and called within minutes. That is the expert path.

caughtGaps.headline: Caught, with gaps
caughtGaps.body: Check how soon you called, whether telemetry and potassium followed, and whether the dose went in.

time_up.body: Suspected digoxin toxicity goes to the provider within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, yellow halos around lights and a slow, irregular apical pulse of 48 in a patient on digoxin are digoxin toxicity until proved otherwise. Her risk is raised by low potassium from the furosemide, worsening kidney function, her age and her low weight. Hold the digoxin, place her on telemetry, and call the provider now for a digoxin level, magnesium and potassium replacement. Giving the dose with an antiemetic would treat the warning sign and add to the toxicity.

riskQ.ask: While the provider reviews her: which lab finding raises the risk of digoxin toxicity?
riskQ.explain: Hypokalemia, hypercalcemia or hypomagnesemia may predispose to digoxin toxicity, as do advanced age, low body weight and impaired renal function.
